questions.stem: When a prokaryotic cell is compared with a eukaryotic cell, which feature is found only in the prokaryote?
options: Ribosomes that carry out protein synthesis in the cytoplasm
A plasma membrane made of a phospholipid bilayer
Linear chromosomes enclosed within a nuclear envelope
A single circular chromosome lying free in the cytoplasm
questions.explanation: Prokaryotes have no nucleus; their DNA is a single circular chromosome in a region of cytoplasm called the nucleoid. Both cell types have ribosomes and a phospholipid plasma membrane. Linear chromosomes inside a nuclear envelope are a eukaryotic feature.

questions.stem: An electron micrograph shows a cell 2 µm long with a cell wall, ribosomes and plasmids, but no membrane-bound organelles. The cell is most likely:
options: a fungal hypha
a human white blood cell
a bacterium
a plant leaf cell
questions.explanation: A small cell with no membrane-bound organelles, and with plasmids, is a prokaryote such as a bacterium. Plant and fungal cells also have cell walls, but they are eukaryotic, so they have a nucleus and other membrane-bound organelles, and they are much larger.

questions.stem: Which organelle modifies, sorts and packages proteins into vesicles for secretion?
options: Smooth endoplasmic reticulum
Lysosome
Nucleus
Golgi apparatus
questions.explanation: The Golgi apparatus receives proteins from the rough ER, modifies them (for example by adding carbohydrate) and packages them into vesicles. Smooth ER makes lipids, and lysosomes digest materials.

questions.stem: Which organelle is the site of aerobic cellular respiration in eukaryotic cells?
options: Chloroplast
Ribosome
Golgi apparatus
Mitochondrion
questions.explanation: Mitochondria carry out the Krebs cycle and electron transport chain, which release most of the energy in glucose as ATP. Chloroplasts carry out photosynthesis, not respiration.

questions.stem: Cells of the human adrenal cortex make large amounts of steroid hormones, which are lipids. Which organelle would be especially abundant in these cells?
options: Smooth endoplasmic reticulum
Rough endoplasmic reticulum
Lysosomes
Chloroplasts
questions.explanation: Smooth ER synthesises lipids, including steroid hormones, so it is extensive in steroid-secreting cells. Rough ER is studded with ribosomes and makes proteins, which suits cells that secrete enzymes or protein hormones instead.

questions.stem: Pancreatic acinar cells secrete large quantities of digestive enzymes. Which pair of organelles would be most prominent in an electron micrograph of these cells?
options: Rough ER and Golgi apparatus
Smooth ER and chloroplasts
Lysosomes and large vacuoles
Smooth ER and lysosomes
questions.explanation: Digestive enzymes are proteins made on the ribosomes of the rough ER and then packaged for secretion by the Golgi apparatus. Smooth ER makes lipids, and animal cells do not have chloroplasts or a large central vacuole.

questions.stem: What is the main function of lysosomes?
options: Breaking down worn-out organelles and engulfed material using enzymes
Storing water and ions to keep the cell turgid
Assembling amino acids into polypeptides
Converting light energy into chemical energy
questions.explanation: Lysosomes are vesicles of hydrolytic enzymes that digest engulfed particles and worn-out organelles. Turgor is maintained by the large vacuole in plant cells, and ribosomes assemble polypeptides.

questions.stem: A cell is found to have chloroplasts, a cell wall and a large central vacuole. Which statement about this cell is correct?
options: It is a plant cell, so it has no need for mitochondria
It is a prokaryote, as cell walls are a prokaryotic feature
It is an animal cell, as all eukaryotes have large vacuoles
It is a plant cell, which also contains mitochondria
questions.explanation: Chloroplasts, a cell wall and a large central vacuole identify a plant cell. Plant cells still need mitochondria, because they respire continually, including at night when photosynthesis stops. Cell walls also occur in fungi and plants, not only prokaryotes.

questions.stem: How do new stem cells arise, and how do they become specialised cells?
options: They are produced by meiosis, then differentiate by losing unneeded genes
They are produced by mitosis, then differentiate by gaining new genes
They are produced by meiosis, then differentiate by fusing with other cells
They are produced by mitosis, then differentiate by expressing particular genes
questions.explanation: Stem cells divide by mitosis, giving genetically identical cells. Differentiation happens as different genes are switched on or off, not by gaining or losing genes; a specialised cell keeps the full genome.

questions.stem: Which type of stem cell can give rise to every cell type of an organism, including the extra-embryonic tissues such as the placenta?
options: Unipotent
Totipotent
Pluripotent
Multipotent
questions.explanation: Totipotent cells, such as the zygote and cells of the very early embryo, can form all cell types including the placenta. Pluripotent cells can form any cell of the body but not the extra-embryonic tissues.

questions.stem: Blood stem cells in bone marrow can form red blood cells, several types of white blood cell and platelets, but not nerve or liver cells. These stem cells are:
options: pluripotent
totipotent
unipotent
multipotent
questions.explanation: A stem cell that can form several related cell types within one tissue family is multipotent. Pluripotent cells could form any body cell, including nerve and liver cells. Unipotent cells form only one cell type.

questions.stem: Stem cells in the basal layer of the skin's epidermis renew themselves and produce only keratinocytes. They are best described as:
options: totipotent
unipotent
multipotent
pluripotent
questions.explanation: A stem cell that self-renews but produces only one type of specialised cell is unipotent. Multipotent cells produce several cell types of one lineage, such as blood stem cells.

questions.stem: Induced pluripotent stem cells are made by reprogramming a patient's own adult skin cells. Compared with embryonic stem cells, a major advantage for repairing that patient's tissues is that they:
options: contain new genes added from the embryo, which improves their differentiation
avoid destroying an embryo and are unlikely to be rejected by the patient's immune system
are totipotent, so they can also form placental tissue for the patient
never divide after being transplanted, so they carry no risk of forming tumours
questions.explanation: Reprogrammed cells come from the patient, so they match the patient's self markers and no embryo is used. They are pluripotent, not totipotent. Like embryonic stem cells, they can divide uncontrollably and form tumours, which is a known safety concern.

questions.stem: Which list is in order of increasing complexity?
options: Cell, organ, tissue, system
Organ, tissue, cell, system
Cell, tissue, organ, system
Tissue, cell, organ, system
questions.explanation: Similar cells form a tissue, different tissues form an organ, and organs working together form a system, such as the digestive system. Each level has properties that its parts do not have on their own.

questions.stem: Oxygen absorbed in the lungs reaches respiring muscle cells. Which pair of body systems work together to achieve this?
options: Digestive and circulatory systems
Respiratory and circulatory systems
Digestive and excretory systems
Respiratory and excretory systems
questions.explanation: The respiratory system brings oxygen to the alveoli, and the circulatory system carries it in the blood to every tissue. The digestive and circulatory systems together supply nutrients rather than gases.

questions.stem: Which statement best explains why sperm cells contain many mitochondria in their midpiece?
options: The tail needs a large supply of ATP for swimming
The mitochondria store the genes passed to the zygote
The mitochondria digest the outer layer of the egg
The midpiece makes the proteins needed by the embryo
questions.explanation: A cell's organelle composition matches its function. Sperm swim by beating the tail, which uses a lot of ATP, so many mitochondria pack the midpiece. Digesting the egg's coat is the job of enzymes in the acrosome.

questions.stem: A red blood cell is a flattened biconcave disc rather than a sphere of the same volume. How does this shape suit its function?
options: It has a smaller SA:V ratio, so it loses less oxygen to the plasma
It has a larger volume, so it can store more haemoglobin per cell
It has a smaller surface area, so it moves faster through capillaries
It has a larger SA:V ratio, so oxygen diffuses in and out faster
questions.explanation: Flattening a cell increases its surface area for the same volume, and no part of the cytoplasm is far from the membrane. Both speed up the diffusion of oxygen. A sphere has the smallest possible surface area for its volume.

questions.stem: A biologist states that a beating heart cannot be explained by studying single cardiac muscle cells alone. Which idea does this illustrate?
options: Cells in an organ are genetically different from one another
Tissues are simpler and therefore more important than organs
Each cell in an organ carries out every function of the organ
New properties emerge at each level of biological organisation
questions.explanation: Scientists study simpler components, but at each level of the hierarchy new properties emerge from the way the parts interact. Coordinated pumping is a property of the whole heart, not of one cell. Cells of an organ share the same genome.

questions.stem: A tissue viewed under a light microscope consists of tightly packed cells forming a continuous sheet that lines a surface, with very little material between the cells. It is most likely:
options: nervous tissue
muscle tissue
epithelial tissue
connective tissue
questions.explanation: Epithelial tissue forms sheets of closely packed cells that cover or line surfaces, such as the alveoli and the gut. Connective tissue, by contrast, has cells scattered through a large amount of extracellular matrix, as in bone, cartilage and blood.

questions.stem: In the fluid mosaic model, what forms the basic structure of the membrane?
options: A rigid layer of cholesterol with proteins attached to it
A bilayer of phospholipids with hydrophobic tails facing inwards
A bilayer of phospholipids with hydrophilic heads facing inwards
A single layer of proteins with lipids embedded in it
questions.explanation: Phospholipids form a bilayer with their hydrophilic phosphate heads facing the watery fluid on each side and their hydrophobic fatty acid tails facing each other inside. Proteins float in this bilayer like a mosaic.

questions.stem: What is the main role of glycoproteins on the outer surface of the cell membrane?
options: Cell recognition and signalling, by acting as markers and receptors
Making the membrane rigid at high temperatures
Pumping ions against their concentration gradients
Forming the hydrophobic core of the bilayer
questions.explanation: Glycoproteins carry carbohydrate chains that act as identity markers and as receptors for signals such as hormones. Cholesterol regulates fluidity, and carrier proteins, not glycoproteins in general, pump ions.

questions.stem: Why is the cell membrane described as fluid?
options: Proteins in the membrane are dissolved in the cytoplasm below it
Phospholipids and many proteins move sideways within the bilayer
The membrane is made mostly of water held between two lipid layers
The membrane dissolves and re-forms each time a substance enters
questions.explanation: Phospholipids and many membrane proteins drift laterally within each layer, so the membrane behaves like a two-dimensional fluid. Cholesterol moderates this movement, keeping the membrane neither too fluid nor too rigid.

questions.stem: What is the role of cholesterol in animal cell membranes?
options: It forms channels that allow ions to cross the membrane by diffusion
It acts as a carrier that binds glucose and moves it across
It forms the hydrophilic outer surface of the phospholipid bilayer
It regulates fluidity, keeping the membrane stable over a range of temperatures
questions.explanation: Cholesterol sits between phospholipid tails. It stops the membrane becoming too fluid when warm and too rigid when cold. Channel and carrier proteins, not cholesterol, move ions and glucose.

questions.stem: Osmosis is best defined as the net movement of:
options: solute across a selectively permeable membrane from higher to lower solute concentration
solute across a selectively permeable membrane using energy from ATP
water across a selectively permeable membrane from lower to higher solute concentration
water across a selectively permeable membrane from higher to lower solute concentration
questions.explanation: In osmosis, water moves across a selectively permeable membrane towards the side with the higher solute concentration, which is the side with less free water. It is passive and needs no ATP.

questions.stem: A red blood cell is placed in distilled water. What happens and why?
options: It stays the same, because its membrane blocks water
It swells and bursts, because water enters by osmosis
It shrinks, because water leaves by osmosis
It swells and bursts, because salt enters by diffusion
questions.explanation: Distilled water is hypotonic to the cytoplasm, so water moves into the cell by osmosis. Animal cells have no cell wall to resist the pressure, so the cell swells and bursts (lysis). A plant cell would become turgid instead.

questions.stem: Which substance crosses the phospholipid bilayer most easily by simple diffusion?
options: Oxygen
Glucose
Sodium ions
Amino acids
questions.explanation: Small non-polar molecules such as oxygen and carbon dioxide dissolve in the hydrophobic core and diffuse straight through. Glucose, amino acids and ions are polar or charged and need channel or carrier proteins.

questions.stem: Glucose enters red blood cells down its concentration gradient through specific carrier proteins, without using ATP. This process is:
options: facilitated diffusion
active transport
simple diffusion
endocytosis
questions.explanation: Movement down a concentration gradient through a protein, with no ATP used, is facilitated diffusion. Active transport also uses carrier proteins but moves substances against their gradient using ATP.

questions.stem: Root hair cells take up nitrate ions from soil even when the nitrate concentration inside the cells is higher than in the soil. Which process is involved, and what does it require?
options: Facilitated diffusion, needing channel proteins only
Osmosis, needing a higher water potential in the cell
Simple diffusion, needing a large surface area only
Active transport, needing carrier proteins and ATP
questions.explanation: Moving ions against their concentration gradient is active transport. It uses specific carrier proteins (pumps) and energy from ATP made in respiration. Diffusion of any kind only moves substances down a gradient.

questions.stem: Root hair cells absorbing nitrate are placed in a solution containing a poison that stops respiration. What is the most likely effect?
options: Nitrate uptake speeds up, because the cell no longer uses nitrate
Nitrate uptake is unaffected, because it occurs by osmosis
Nitrate uptake continues, because carrier proteins need no energy
Nitrate uptake against the gradient stops, because no ATP is made
questions.explanation: Active transport depends on ATP from respiration, so a respiratory poison stops uptake against the gradient. Passive processes such as diffusion would continue, but they cannot move nitrate into a cell that already has more of it.

questions.stem: A white blood cell surrounds a bacterium with its membrane and takes it in within a vesicle. This process is:
options: exocytosis
facilitated diffusion
osmosis
endocytosis
questions.explanation: Endocytosis takes large particles or fluid into the cell by enfolding them in the membrane to form a vesicle; engulfing a solid particle is called phagocytosis. Exocytosis is the reverse, releasing vesicle contents from the cell.

questions.stem: How do nerve cells release neurotransmitters, and how is this classed?
options: Vesicles fuse with the membrane in endocytosis, a form of passive transport
Molecules diffuse through channels in exocytosis, a form of passive transport
Molecules leave through carrier proteins in osmosis, a form of active transport
Vesicles fuse with the membrane in exocytosis, a form of active transport
questions.explanation: Neurotransmitters are packed in vesicles that fuse with the plasma membrane and release their contents outside: exocytosis. Bulk transport by vesicles uses ATP, so it is classed as active transport.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly compares active and passive transport?
options: Passive transport moves substances against a gradient using ATP; active transport moves them down one without ATP
Passive transport occurs only in plant cells; active transport occurs only in animal cells with no cell wall
Passive transport moves substances down a gradient without ATP; active transport can move them against one using ATP
Passive transport always needs membrane proteins; active transport moves substances straight through the bilayer
questions.explanation: Passive processes (simple and facilitated diffusion, osmosis) move substances down their concentration gradient using only kinetic energy. Active transport and bulk transport use ATP and can move substances against a gradient. Simple diffusion needs no protein at all.

questions.stem: What is the surface area to volume ratio of a cube with sides of 3 cm?
questions.explanation: Surface area = 6 × 3 × 3 = 54 cm² and volume = 3 × 3 × 3 = 27 cm³, so SA:V = 54 : 27 = 2 : 1. A 1 cm cube has 6 : 1 and a 2 cm cube has 3 : 1, so the ratio falls as size increases.

questions.stem: A student asks why cells do not simply keep growing larger instead of dividing. Which is the best explanation?
options: Larger cells have a larger SA:V ratio, so they lose materials too quickly
Larger cells cannot fit enough DNA into a nucleus of normal size
Larger cells have membranes that are too thick for substances to cross
Larger cells have a smaller SA:V ratio, so diffusion cannot meet their needs
questions.explanation: As a cell grows, its volume (which sets its demand) increases faster than its surface area (which sets its supply). Diffusion over longer distances is also slow. Beyond a certain size, exchange across the membrane cannot keep up.

questions.stem: Agar cubes of side 1 cm, 2 cm and 3 cm containing a pink indicator are placed in acid for 10 minutes. The acid removes the colour to a depth of 0.4 cm in every cube. Which conclusion is supported?
options: The 1 cm cube had the largest percentage of its volume reached by the acid
The 3 cm cube had the largest percentage of its volume reached by the acid
The acid diffused faster into the 1 cm cube, as shown by the depth reached
All three cubes had the same percentage of their volume reached by the acid
questions.explanation: The depth reached was the same, so the rate of diffusion was the same in each cube. But about 99% of the 1 cm cube was decolourised, compared with about 78% of the 2 cm cube and about 61% of the 3 cm cube, because the smaller cube has the larger SA:V ratio.

questions.stem: In the agar cube experiment, which change would most improve the reliability of the conclusion about SA:V ratio?
options: Cutting each cube by eye to save time in preparation
Leaving each cube in the acid for a different time
Repeating each cube size several times and averaging the results
Using a stronger acid so the colour change is faster
questions.explanation: Replicates reduce the effect of random error and show whether results are consistent, which improves reliability. Changing the timing for each cube would introduce an uncontrolled variable and reduce validity.

questions.stem: A light microscope has a 10× eyepiece and is used with a 40× objective lens. What is the total magnification?
questions.explanation: Total magnification = eyepiece magnification × objective magnification = 10 × 40 = 400×. Adding the two values (50×) is a common slip.

questions.stem: At a total magnification of 40×, the field of view is 4.5 mm in diameter. At 400×, 9 cells fit end to end across the field of view. What is the approximate length of one cell?
options: 50 µm
500 µm
5 µm
0.5 µm
questions.explanation: Increasing magnification ten times reduces the field of view ten times: 4.5 mm ÷ 10 = 0.45 mm = 450 µm. Each cell is 450 ÷ 9 = 50 µm long. Forgetting to shrink the field of view gives 500 µm.

questions.stem: Why are electron micrographs, rather than light micrographs, used to compare the organelle composition of different cell types?
options: Electron microscopes can view living cells, so organelles can be seen moving
Electron micrographs show true colours, so organelles are easy to identify
Electron microscopes have a wider field of view, so whole tissues are seen
Electron microscopes have much higher resolution, so small organelles can be seen
questions.explanation: Electron microscopes resolve detail far finer than light microscopes, revealing ribosomes, ER and the internal structure of mitochondria. Specimens must be dead and prepared in a vacuum, and the images have no true colour.

questions.stem: Researchers studying tissue repair replace some animal experiments with cell cultures and use fewer animals by improving their statistics. Which principles are they applying?
options: Respect and refinement
Replacement and reduction
Replacement and refinement
Reduction and refinement
questions.explanation: The three Rs are replacement (using alternatives such as cell cultures), reduction (using fewer animals) and refinement (lessening pain and distress). The changes described are replacement and reduction.
